A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same self-jailbreaking study and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite appendix renumbering and layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, self-jailbreaking annotations, activation projection and steering experiments, and safety-training results in Sections 3–5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds counterfactual experiments, type-level analyses, Llama safety-training evaluations and adversarial benchmark comparisons.

M1.justification: The activation-direction extraction, steering procedure and minimal safety-training recipe remain unchanged. The Llama experiments apply the existing training mixture; sentence regeneration is introduced as an experimental control, not a revised mitigation algorithm.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds Wild Jailbreak and evaluates mitigation under adaptive, past-tense and prefilling attacks on StrongREJECT. This substantially extends the mitigation's evaluated input conditions beyond v1's unmodified harmful prompts. v1's separate experiment transferring self-jailbreaking sentences to other models is retained.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 introduces evaluated comparisons against STAR, SafeChain, DAPO and RECAP on StrongREJECT and Wild Jailbreak. v1 discussed related safety-training work but did not provide this comparison against dedicated competing methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds a counterfactual protocol on 102 annotated instances, regenerating self-jailbreaking sentences while holding preceding reasoning fixed. It also introduces manual type-classification sampling across five models and Llama-3-8B training/evaluation configurations. The existing 500-token safety and 8000-token capability evaluation limits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.2 adds a controlled test of sentence-level effects. Appendix F adds rationalization-type frequencies and type-specific activation changes, distinct from the retained prompt-topic distribution. Appendix G adds mitigation generalization to Llama and robustness tests against external jailbreaks.

E5.justification: v1 already reports graphical error bars, which v2 retains. The new ± entries in Tables 1 and 4 accompany additional results without documenting a different uncertainty-estimation practice. Neither version specifies seeds, repeated-run counts, significance tests or the meaning of these uncertainty measures.

E6.justification: v2 Table 1 newly reports compliance/harmfulness changes of 3.1/-2.9 for self-jailbreaking versus -0.2/0.1 for counterfactuals. Tables 4–6 add type-specific, adversarial and baseline results; Table 5 reports StrongREJECT ASRs of 81.7% for Distilled-Llama-8B and 8.1% for SAFE-LLAMA-8B. Original plotted results are retained; these are added comparisons, not improvements to the same v1 measurements.

T1.justification: The self-jailbreaking definition, projection normalization and activation-steering equations are unchanged. The counterfactual experiment uses the existing projection quantities and introduces no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statement and conclusion retain the same claims: benign reasoning training induces self-jailbreaking, increased compliance and reduced perceived harmfulness explain it, and minimal safety reasoning mitigates it while preserving reasoning capability. New experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: Appendix G newly identifies weaker robustness on Wild Jailbreak, motivates incorporating adversarial safety data and acknowledges that the reported results are not best among competing methods. Appendix F adds tentative explanations linking type distributions to training and architecture. These extend the applicability discussion without replacing the central mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 provides more specific training-data provenance for existing models, including RStar-Coder's code data and UniReason's 47K math samples. It also describes the s1 and STAR mixture used for the new Llama experiments. These are limited documentation additions, not evidence that the retained models were retrained differently.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for WildTeaming, past-tense and priming attacks, and training-data sources. Section 4.1.1 more explicitly positions the analysis as extending Zhao et al.'s separation of harmfulness and refusal to reasoning models. The broader positioning remains stable; the adaptive-attack reference is a publication update.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized explanatory rewrites, adds Appendices F and G, removes the contents page and relabels the retained appendices. The main section sequence and most prose remain intact, so this is not an extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: New Tables 1 and 4–6 present counterfactual effects, type-specific effects, adversarial evaluations and competing-method comparisons; new Figure 13 displays rationalization-type frequencies. These substantially expand the quantitative presentation. Original figures remain, with some relocation and surrounding layout changes.

improvement.justification: The matched-prefix counterfactual experiment strengthens causal support beyond v1's projection and steering evidence. Type-level analysis and Llama, adversarial and competing-method evaluations address important gaps in the mitigation's validation, while revealing its limits rather than merely reporting successes. Undefined uncertainty summaries and sparse details for the new comparisons remain weaknesses, but the added controls and broader validation substantially improve the paper's evidential foundation.
